html:
A US law of 6 June 1934 that set up the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to police the stock market. It followed the Securities Act of 1933, which made companies selling new shares publish honest facts about them.

Before these laws, American markets had few rules. Insiders ran pools to push up prices, and companies could tell investors almost anything. The 1929 crash and the Pecora hearings showed the scale of abuse.

The 1934 act required public companies to report regularly, banned market manipulation and insider fraud, and put exchanges such as the New York Stock Exchange and brokers under federal supervision. Roosevelt picked Joseph P. Kennedy, a former stock speculator, as the first chairman, reasoning that he knew every trick.

With Glass-Steagall, the acts form the base of the New Deal's control of finance. The SEC still regulates US securities markets.
